title: Different Roads, Same Destination
about: What happens when pieces take different routes or get lost.

cards.title: The internet makes no promises
cards.body: [[Routers|router]] keep updating their [[routing tables|routing-table]]. If a cable breaks or a road gets busy, they find another way round. So packets from one message can take different roads and arrive in a **different order**. Some never arrive at all. Yet your photos always turn up perfectly. How?

cards.prompt: The cable from **Router A** straight to the web [[server]] has been cut, so it's no longer on the map. Get the [[packet]] to the **web server** another way.
cards.explanation: Either detour works: through **Router B**, or through **Router A** and on to **Router C**. A broken cable doesn't stop the whole internet, because routers simply send packets another way. But if some packets take one road and some take the other, they may arrive in a different order.
cards.hint: The cut cable is gone from the map, so only follow the links you can see. There's more than one way round.
cards.nudge: Check that every step follows a line on the map. The link from [[Router]] A straight to the server has been removed.

cards.prompt: These [[packets|packet]] took different roads and arrived jumbled up. Use their **sequence numbers** to put them back in order.
cards.explanation: Sorting by sequence number gives **#1, #2, #3, #4**: *YOUR PIZZA IS ARRIVING*. The receiver doesn't care what order packets turn up in. The sequence numbers say where each piece belongs.
cards.hint: The order they arrived in is no help. What did the sender put on every packet so the receiver could do this job?
cards.nudge: Sort by the number after the #, from smallest to largest. The order they arrived in doesn't matter.

cards.prompt:
For web pages, photos and downloads, computers follow a set of rules called **TCP** (Transmission Control [[Protocol]]). TCP numbers the packets, and the receiver keeps telling the sender which ones have arrived. Any gap gets sent again.

A message was sent as packets 1 to 7. Packets **1, 2, 4, 6 and 7** arrived. **How many** packets will TCP send again?
cards.explanation: The [[sequence numbers|sequence-number]] jump from 2 to 4 and from 4 to 6, so **packets 3 and 5** are missing: **2** packets. Only those two are sent again. The receiver keeps the other five and slots 3 and 5 in when they arrive. Put together: IP gets packets across the internet, and TCP makes sure they all arrive, in the right order.
cards.hint: Write out 1 to 7, then cross off each number that arrived. Count what's left.
cards.nudge: There may be more than one gap. Check every number from 1 to 7, and count the ones that never arrived.

cards.prompt: Match each problem to how the internet deals with it.

pairs.left: A cable on the route breaks

cards.explanation: Out-of-order packets are **sorted** using their sequence numbers. A missing packet is **sent again**, thanks to [[TCP]]. And when a cable on the route breaks, routers [[update]] their tables and **send packets another way**.
cards.hint: Think about which fix uses sequence numbers, which one sends a piece again, and which one is a job for routers.
cards.nudge: Sequence numbers fix order, resending fixes a missing piece, and routers deal with problems along the road.

cards.prompt: On a video call, a lost packet makes the picture glitch for a moment. The call doesn't pause to wait for the packet to be sent again. Why not?

options.text: Waiting would make the call lag. For live video, fresh data is more useful than late data
Video calls send one continuous stream instead of packets, so there's nothing to resend
options.nudge: Everything on the internet travels in packets, video calls included.

options.text: Video packets have extra protection, so they can never actually be lost
options.nudge: Any packet can go missing, video ones too. The question says a lost packet caused the glitch.

options.text: Video packets are far too big to be sent a second time
options.nudge: Packet size isn't the reason. Think about timing: what happens to a live call while it waits?

cards.explanation: In a live call, a packet that arrives half a second late is useless: that moment has already passed. So live apps usually skip lost packets and keep going, often using simpler rules called **UDP**, which don't resend anything. A face frozen mid-sneeze for a split second beats the whole call stopping to wait. For a download, it's the other way round: every [[byte]] has to be perfect, so [[TCP]] waits and resends.
cards.hint: In a live call, what's the use of a picture from half a second ago that turns up late?

cards.prompt: Yesterday's [[traceroute]] to example.com is saved at the top of the [[terminal]]. Run `traceroute example.com` now and compare the two, [[hop]] by hop (the numbered lines). One hop has changed.
cards.intro:
Saved from yesterday:

$ traceroute example.com
traceroute to example.com (198.51.100.10), 30 hops max, 60 byte packets
 1  192.168.1.1 (192.168.1.1)  1.912 ms  1.804 ms  1.765 ms
 2  203.0.113.1 (203.0.113.1)  9.483 ms  9.412 ms  9.377 ms
 3  203.0.113.65 (203.0.113.65)  11.207 ms  11.164 ms  11.122 ms
 4  198.51.100.1 (198.51.100.1)  18.930 ms  18.842 ms  19.004 ms
 5  example.com (198.51.100.10)  19.315 ms  19.271 ms  19.233 ms

Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: List each router between you and example.com, right now

success.question: What is the address of the router that's on today's route but wasn't on yesterday's?

cards.explanation: Hop 3 was `203.0.113.65` yesterday and is `203.0.113.129` today. Every other hop is the same. Maybe the old [[router]] was busy or being repaired, so traffic was sent another way. The detour is a little slower (about 22 ms to the end instead of 19 ms), but your [[packets|packet]] still get there.
cards.hint: Run `traceroute example.com`, then compare the address on each numbered line with yesterday's, one line at a time.
cards.nudge: The times change a little on every line, so compare only the addresses. Give the address that appears today, not yesterday's.

cards.title: Recap: Packets and Routing
cards.body:
- Routes can change, so packets may arrive jumbled or go missing.
- **Sequence numbers** put the pieces back in order.
- **TCP** gets any missing packet sent again.
